reason: A four-word run and a KJV singleton — “their armies to battle” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the singleton is arithmetic rather than evidential. The King James Bible narrates armies going to battle constantly and simply had occasion to phrase it with this possessive once. 1 Samuel 17:1 is the muster before David and Goliath; Mormon 4:1 is the Nephites' opening offensive of the year 363, and nothing else of 1 Samuel 17 is present — no champion, no single combat, no defiance. The Book of Mormon uses the same construction throughout the war books (Alma 43, Mormon 2-6), so it is the corpus's own military idiom, not a borrowing from the one KJV verse that shares the possessive.

The machine's highest-ranked candidate at three separate verses of this chapter (4:2, 4:7, 4:13), on the strength of “take possession of the” plus “and it came to pass”. It is boilerplate on both sides. 1 Kings 21:15 is Jezebel telling Ahab to seize Naboth's vineyard; the Book of Mormon phrase is its standard verb for the capture of a fortified city and occurs across Alma and Mormon dozens of times. The only feature that could tempt is that Naboth's vineyard is a seizure by murder and Mormon 4 is a chapter of seizure by massacre, but there is no shared vocabulary beyond the formula and no vineyard, no false witness, no prophetic sentence. This entry covers 4:7 and 4:13 as well; they are not listed individually.

sharedText: boast of their strength ... in their own might
reason: NOT a rejection — a placement note. Mormon 4:8's “they did again boast of their strength; and they went forth in their own might” is the Book of Mormon's boasting-in-own-strength doctrine, whose KJV footing was argued at Helaman 4:13 (“their boastings in their own strength, they were left in their own strength”), where the noun “boastings” is a King James singleton at James 4:16. Mormon 4:8 has the verb, not the noun, so the singleton that carries the Helaman row is not present here and a fresh link would rest on nothing. “Their own strength” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses and “own strength” in exactly two, Psalm 21:13 and Amos 6:13, neither of which is about a nation boasting after a victory. Deuteronomy 8:17's “the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth” — also a singleton — was weighed as the alternative and declined: it is about wealth, not arms, and shares no word with 4:8. A reader who wants the biblical background of this sentence should be sent to Helaman 4:13.

“Every heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 21:7, and the temptation is sharp, because Ezekiel 21 is the sword-song — “A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished” — and is therefore the KJV chapter closest in subject to Mormon 4. But the predicate is exactly inverted. Ezekiel's every heart shall MELT, with all hands feeble and all knees weak as water, at the mere news that the sword is coming; Mormon's every heart WAS HARDENED, so that they delighted in the shedding of blood continually. Ezekiel describes a people undone by the prospect of slaughter; Mormon describes a people who have acquired a taste for it. Two words, opposed verbs, and the whole difference between the two chapters' anthropology lies in that opposition. Recorded because the singleton would otherwise look overlooked, and because the inversion is more interesting than the parallel would have been.

“It is impossible for the tongue to describe, or for man to write a perfect description” is an inexpressibility topos, and the King James Bible has two famous ones: John 21:25, whose “the world itself” is a singleton — “even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written” — and Romans 8:26's “groanings which cannot be uttered”, also a singleton. Neither is present in any word. John's topos is about superabundance of good (the deeds of Jesus), Romans' about prayer beyond language; Mormon's is about the unspeakability of atrocity, which the KJV never has occasion to say. The Book of Mormon uses the figure repeatedly in its own words (3 Nephi 17:17, “no tongue can speak”), so it is a corpus habit rather than a borrowing. Recorded because a reader meeting a sentence about what cannot be written will think of John 21:25, and should be told the catalogue thought of it too.

NOT a rejection — a cross-reference. 4:14 is the first of the chapter's two child-sacrifice notices (“did take many prisoners of women and of children, and did offer them up as sacrifices unto their idol gods”), and it is the one a reader will stop at. Its wording, however, is the Book of Mormon's own: “idol gods” is in no KJV verse, and “sacrificed unto” alone occurs in ten, too many to identify a source. The KJV wording appears at 4:21, “sacrificed unto idols”, against Psalm 106:38's “sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan”, which is a King James singleton — so the link is filed there, where the words are (CONVENTIONS §6a), and covers both notices. Ezekiel 16:20-21 and 2 Kings 17:17 were weighed here and share no wording with either verse.

“They were not numbered, because of the greatness of their number” is the innumerable-army topos, and the KJV has a well-stocked shelf of it: Judges 6:5 and 7:12's Midianites “as grasshoppers for multitude ... without number”, 1 Kings 3:8's people “that cannot be numbered nor counted for multitude”, Genesis 32:12's sand of the sea. “Not be numbered” is even a KJV singleton, at Genesis 16:10. None of them is here. Every KJV instance pairs the countlessness with a simile — grasshoppers, sand, stars — and Mormon 4:17 supplies no simile at all, only the flat tautology that they could not be counted because there were too many. The candidate is a topos held in common, not a text used, and the Gideon parallel that the topos suggests (a small covenant force against an innumerable host) is precisely the shape Mormon 4 refuses: there is no Gideon here and the small force loses.

A four-word run scoring at the top of the verse, and the two senses of “beat” have nothing to do with each other. Exodus 39:3 is the making of the high priest's ephod: “they did beat the gold into thin plates, and cut it into wires, to work it in the blue, and in the purple, and in the scarlet.” Mormon 4:19 is a rout: “an exceeding sore battle fought in the land Desolation, in the which they did beat the Nephites.” Metalworking against military defeat, with the object supplying the whole difference. Worth the entry only because “beat ... into thin plates” sits so close to the Book of Mormon's own governing metaphor of engraved plates that a reader running a concordance on plates and beating will land here; there is no connection, and the plates of Mormon 4:23 are taken up, not hammered.

“Great slaughter” occurs in fifteen KJV verses and is the standard formula of the conquest and early monarchy narratives — Joshua at Gibeon, Jephthah at Minnith, Samson hip and thigh, David against the Philistines. No single verse can be the source and none is proposed. It is worth recording what the formula does here rather than where it comes from: in the KJV the great slaughter is almost always inflicted BY the covenant people ON the nations, and the one conspicuous exception, 1 Samuel 4:10, is the day the ark was taken. Mormon 4:21 puts the covenant people on the receiving end of their own scriptural idiom, and follows it immediately with their children sacrificed to idols. The reversal is the interesting fact; a link is not.
